questions.learningObjective: Explain the performance trade-off between subquery and join
questions.stem: Cartographer's projection: analyst chooses between a subquery filter and a join

options.text: Stage one: always use subquery; stage two: joins are unsafe
options.misconception: claims joins are always unsafe

options.text: Stage one: always use join; stage two: subqueries are obsolete
options.misconception: claims subqueries are obsolete

options.text: Stage one: use subquery for membership only; stage two: use join when columns are needed
Stage one: use cross join; stage two: filter manually
options.misconception: uses cartesian product instead of a key join

questions.explanation: Subqueries suit membership tests and avoid multiplication; joins are needed for columns. Neither is always better, and cross joins are not a substitute.
questions.hint: Match the tool to the need.

questions.stem: Cartographer's projection: an order has a customer_id not present in customers

answer.exemplar: The inner join drops that order because there is no matching customer row, so unmatched left rows disappear.

questions.explanation: An inner join requires a match in both tables, so unmatched left rows are dropped. The tempting idea that they are kept with nulls describes a left join instead.
questions.hint: No match means dropped in inner join.

questions.stem: Cartographer's projection: analyst Veda suspects a join multiplied rows

options.text: Stage one: count distinct left keys; stage two: ignore right side
options.misconception: ignores the right side's role in multiplication

options.text: Stage one: rerun the query; stage two: assume correctness if it runs

questions.explanation: Comparing result to left count and checking right key uniqueness detects multiplication. Rerunning, ignoring the right side, or post-hoc filtering does not diagnose it.

questions.explanation: A filter subquery tests membership, so duplicates in the subquery do not multiply outer rows. The tempting idea that duplicates multiply confuses subquery filters with joins.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Subquery in a filter versus a join
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a subquery in a filter differs from a join in row count
questions.stem: Cartographer's projection: analyst replaces a join with a filter subquery

options.text: Stage one: row count is unchanged; stage two: columns are still added
options.misconception: thinks subquery adds columns and preserves count

options.text: Stage one: row count always increases; stage two: all right columns appear
options.misconception: thinks subquery behaves like a join

options.text: Stage one: row count may decrease; stage two: no right columns are added
Stage one: result is empty; stage two: nothing is returned
options.misconception: thinks replacing join with subquery empties result

questions.explanation: A filter subquery tests membership and does not add columns, so row count may drop if some rows fail the test and no right columns appear. It does not inflate, add columns, or empty the result by default.
